title: Your hukam, daily
hookLine: keep reading the Guru's order each morning
tomorrow: Simran has to bring her own ardas. where does she even start?

lines: WHO READS THIS TO YOU IN THE FALL?
WHAT IF I DON'T LIKE IT?
cards: The kitchen light is on and the sun isn't. Bebe Jaswant sits at the table in her shawl, phone held at arm's length, reading out the day's hukam from Darbar Sahib, line by slow line.
On the fridge behind her, under a chili-shaped magnet, is Simran's college letter. Simran pours tea and half listens, the way she has for years.

Then Bebe stops mid-line, slides the phone across the table, and says: in the fall, who reads this to you? Simran picks it up and asks the thing she's never said out loud. What if it says something I don't want to hear?

teach.b: Bebe's answer starts with the word. Hukam means order, command: the way things are ordered, and the word that orders them. Guru Nanak sets it near the very start of the Japji, on Ang 1.
In paraphrase: everyone is within the hukam; no one stands outside it. So the daily hukam isn't a fortune. It doesn't promise a good day or warn you off a bad one.
It's a line of the Guru's word, given for today. Here's how it's taken.
The Sikh code of conduct describes it: open the Guru Granth Sahib and read the hymn at the top of the left-hand page; if it began on the page before, turn back and read it from its start.
And here's one to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: NOT READ IT. WALK IN IT.
teach.b: The Japji's first pauri ends on this word, and the verb isn't read. In paraphrase: walk in the hukam, the will; Nanak, it's written with you. Not read it.
So what if it's hard? Then it's hard, Bebe says, and you walk anyway, with it in your pocket. You don't open the book again to find a nicer one.
Simran sets an alarm for the dark hour and names it: hukam.

how: Sikhs take a hukam by opening the Guru Granth Sahib and reading the hymn at the top of the left-hand page; some families also follow the morning hukam read at Darbar Sahib in Amritsar, at home or on a phone.

o: a fortune told from a page opened at random each day
the Guru's word for the day, read each morning to walk in
a rule list the gurdwara committee posts every week

games.q: the morning order — tap the pairs.
p: order: the way things are ordered
where the day's hukam is read from
no one stands outside the order
walk in the hukam; it's written with you

s: the daily hukam is a forecast of how your day will go
it's a line of the Guru's word to walk in, not a prediction.
the hukam is read from the top of the left-hand page
and if the hymn began on the page before, you turn back to its start.
if the hukam is hard, you open the book again for a better one
Bebe's answer: it's hard, and you walk with it anyway.

games.q: your cousin reads the day's hukam and it's about death. he wants to open the Granth again for something cheerful. what does the practice say?
o: open again; a hard hukam can't be meant for a good day.
keep this one; it's today's order, to walk in, not to pick.
skip it today; a hard hukam means wait until tomorrow.
games.why: the code says read the hymn at the top of the left-hand page. it isn't chosen for comfort; it's the line you walk in today.

practice: If you can, find today's hukam from Darbar Sahib and read it slowly, once, in whatever language you can. If not, stay with the Japji's line instead: everyone is within the order.
Choose one phrase from what you read and say it under your breath on each out-breath until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Your hukam: the Guru's order for the day, read from the top of the left-hand page, and carried, not just read.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: hukam, order or command; the hukamnama is the day's order from the Granth.

carryVoice: The line to keep: my daily order, read in the dark and walked in by daylight. See you at first light.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Japji, pauri 1: walk in the hukam, the will, it is written with you; pauri 2: all are within the hukam, none outside it), paraphrased
Sikh Rehat Maryada, section on taking the hukam (read the hymn at the top of the left-hand page; if it begins on the previous page, turn back to its start), paraphrased
